subject: Help estimating conditional autoregressive models other than intrinisic CAR

messages.author: 5b5ac0e901ae0add
messages.subject: Help estimating conditional autoregressive models other than intrinisic CAR
parts:
I'd like to specify a model in R-INLA that includes a general CAR random effect with (possibly) asymmetric weights and (possibly) non-constant conditional variances. 
For example, if I wanted to fit a spatial random effect where the conditional densities y.i | y.j are distributed N(sum(b.ij * y.j) , tau.i**2), what would the INLA model syntax look like? 
 
Assuming the known and fixed set of b.ij and tau.i produce a compatible, nonsingular MV density, is such a model possible currently in R-INLA?  Is there documentation or an example you could direct me to? 
 
Thank you.

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a

> I'd like to specify a model in R-INLA that includes a general CAR
> random effect with (possibly) asymmetric weights and (possibly)
> non-constant conditional variances.
> For example, if I wanted to fit a spatial random effect where the
> conditional densities y.i | y.j are distributed N(sum(b.ij * y.j) ,
> tau.i**2), what would the INLA model syntax look like?
>
> Assuming the known and fixed set of b.ij and tau.i produce a
> compatible, nonsingular MV density, is such a model possible currently
> in R-INLA? Is there documentation or an example you could direct me
> to?
>

Hi.

There are the generic model-class that can deal with arbitrary weights,
but the site-spesific conditional precision, is harder. This is because
they goes into the hyperparameters and not the Gaussian part, and there
is not obvious way how these should be parameterized.

For known {b.ij and tau.i}, then its ok; see

inla.doc("generic")

and the case where

tau.i = kappa * tau.i.fixed

where 'kappa' is unknown, is also covered in that model. "generic1" is
another variant.

If you have some other spesific model in mind that is not covered here;
please let us know.


--

messages.author: 5b5ac0e901ae0add
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Help estimating conditional autoregressive models other than intrinisic CAR
parts:
Thanks for the response.  Could you clarify a few more things for me.
 
How would I incorporate the weights (the b.ij) in the generic models?  These weights are stored in an asymmetric sparse matrix.  Will f() accept a sparse weight matrix?
I would like to estimate the kappa parameter mentioned above.  This would be equivalent to the tau effect (not to be confused with tau.i above) listed in the generic model examples, right? And the C matrix for the model posted above would be equivalent to a diagonal with entries 1/tau.i**2?  OR would the C matrix need to be the precision matrix for the full MV density covariance matrix (and, thus, negate the use of the conditional weight matrix)?  If the latter is true, how would you recommend I calculate that precision matrix for large sparse covariance matrices?

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Help estimating conditional autoregressive models other than intrinisic CAR

> Thanks for the response. Could you clarify a few more things for me.
>
> How would I incorporate the weights (the b.ij) in the generic models?
> These weights are stored in an asymmetric sparse matrix. Will f()

you have to give the precision matrix. how the precision matrix relates
to your b.ij weights and tau.i is explained in the attached document,
thm 2.6.

> I would like to estimate the kappa parameter mentioned above. This
> would be equivalent to the tau effect (not to be confused with tau.i
> above) listed in the generic model examples, right?

yes. you can still have different tau.i, as long as they all scale with
one common (possibly) unknown kappa.

> And the C matrix for the model posted above would be equivalent to a
> diagonal with entries 1/tau.i**2?
The C-matrix is proportional to the precision matrix.

> If the latter is true, how would you recommend I calculate that
> precision matrix for large sparse covariance matrices?

If you have a spatial model given by a covariance function, then its a
different issue; see


https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/www/faq#TOC-I-have-used-R-INLA-in-scientific-wo

and the Lindgren reference. INLA has support for these kind of models as
well...

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Help estimating conditional autoregressive models other than intrinisic CAR
parts:
On Thursday, 15 March 2012 08:43:01 UTC+1, help help wrote:
> How would I incorporate the weights (the b.ij) in the generic models?
> These weights are stored in an asymmetric sparse matrix.  Will f()
> accept a sparse weight matrix?

you have to give the precision matrix. how the precision matrix relates
to your b.ij weights and tau.i is explained in the attached document,
thm 2.6.

Adding to this, if your conditional weight matrix [b.ij] is sparse, then the precision matrix will be sparse, as shown in the pdf file
The covariance matrix is the inverse of the precision, and will _not_ be sparse.  Conversely, if your covariance matrix is sparse, then your conditional weight matrix cannot have been sparse.  Inla handles sparse precision matrixes, but not large sparse covariance matrices.  In your case, it seems you have sparse weights, and hence a sparse precision, so everything should be fine.

Secondly, the spatial SPDE models as implemented by inla can actually be used as "more generic" precision models for other types of problems as well (though this is as yet undocumented).  If you cannot write your model on the "generic0" or "generic1" forms, let us know precisely what precision model you need, and we'll be able to tell you if there is an implementation available.

/Finn Lindgren
